tldr: To successfully transfer policies from simulation to real-world torque-controlled robots (Sim2Real), this paper proposes a "Real2Sim2Real" pipeline that combines genetic algorithm-based dynamics identification using real trajectories with domain randomization. On a real 7-DOF arm, the authors demonstrate the stable real-world transfer of reinforcement learning policies trained directly on torque commands in simulation.
hero_caption: Overall view of the proposed Real2Sim2Real pipeline. Trajectory data from the real robot is used to identify friction and inertia parameters (Real2Sim). Reinforcement learning is then performed in the high-fidelity simulator combined with domain randomization, followed by intermediate validation in Gazebo before safely deploying the policy to the real robot.
overview:
To achieve both delicate and compliant contact tasks with a robotic arm, low-level joint torque control is ideal. However, training reinforcement learning (RL) policies with direct torque control on real robots risks hardware damage, raises safety concerns, and takes massive amounts of time. Therefore, Sim2Real—training policies in a physics simulator and transferring them to the real robot—is commonly used. But in torque control, even tiny modeling errors in friction and inertia can be fatal, causing the "reality gap" to trigger severe oscillations or complete stalls on the physical hardware.

To solve this, the authors conceived a "Real2Sim2Real" pipeline that estimates the simulator's physical parameters from real-world data to improve model fidelity before performing reinforcement learning and domain randomization. Rather than relying on default robot description files (such as URDFs), they used trajectory data from moving the real arm together with a genetic algorithm (GA) to thoroughly identify direction-dependent kinetic friction coefficients, static friction, gravity compensation offsets, and link inertia tensors. Inside this calibrated simulator, they trained reaching tasks using TQC, an RL algorithm well-suited for continuous action spaces.

For evaluation, they first conducted Sim2Sim verification between two different physics engines, MuJoCo and Gazebo, and finally deployed the policy onto a real 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda robot. While uncalibrated models showed complete discrepancies in torques and motion between simulation and reality, policies trained in the calibrated environment reached target positions extremely smoothly on the real robot without any oscillations.
contributions: Established a high-accuracy dynamics identification method (Real2Sim) for low-level torque-controlled manipulators by combining real-world trajectory matching with a genetic algorithm.
Constructed a high-fidelity simulation environment incorporating direction-dependent kinetic friction, experimentally measured static friction thresholds, and gravity compensation offsets.
Achieved zero-shot, stable transfer of control policies to both Sim2Sim (MuJoCo to Gazebo) and the real robot (Sim2Real) using the TQC algorithm paired with a smoothness-promoting reward design.

sections.heading: Why is Sim2Real so difficult with torque control?
sections.summary: Joint torque control is ideal for compliant environmental interaction, but simulation is essential because direct RL on real robots is dangerous. However, physical discrepancies between simulation and reality (the reality gap) often cause simulation-trained policies to fail on hardware. This work tackles this issue using a Real2Sim2Real pipeline combining real-world identification with reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
When a robot performs tasks involving physical contact with its environment, directly commanding joint torques is far more promising than position control because it can compliantly adapt to external forces. However, optimizing torque commands through trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) directly on a real robot is extremely hazardous due to risks of equipment damage and human safety, not to mention the immense time required.

Consequently, the standard approach is Sim2Real transfer: safely and rapidly training a policy in simulation first, then porting it to the real machine. The major roadblock here is the physical discrepancy between simulation and the real world—the "reality gap." In position control, internal motor servo loops can reject disturbances to some extent. In torque control, however, even minor errors in friction, moments of inertia, or gravity compensation directly impact the robot's physical behavior. As a result, policies that worked flawlessly in simulation frequently end up shuddering, vibrating, or failing to reach targets once placed on physical hardware.

Against this backdrop, this study targets the 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda arm and proposes an integrated framework combining calibration techniques that bring the simulator as close to real behavior as possible with robust RL. The core focus here is laying solid groundwork: ensuring that torque control policies in free space, prior to environmental contact, can transfer stably onto the real machine.

sections.heading: Two main approaches to closing the reality gap and their limitations
sections.summary: Bridging the sim-to-real gap typically relies on domain randomization (varying physical parameters) or trajectory matching (fitting simulation to real data). To handle complex motor characteristics and coupling in torque control, these approaches must be combined appropriately. This paper positions its method as layering domain randomization on top of GA-based trajectory identification.
sections.details:
Training robots directly in joint space allows full utilization of robot dynamics, yielding superior performance in contact tasks. However, its success heavily depends on the accuracy of the physics model inside the simulator. To overcome this reality gap, two primary approaches have been investigated.

The first is Domain Randomization (DR). By intentionally randomizing simulation parameters such as friction, mass, and link inertia during training, the policy learns to be robust against real-world variations and uncertainties. While powerful and widely adopted, DR has a major drawback: if the baseline values in the simulator diverge significantly from the real robot, no amount of randomization will properly cover the real dynamics, making learning convergence difficult.

The second is Trajectory Matching. This approach inversely identifies physical parameters by minimizing the error between joint trajectory data captured from the real robot and the simulator's response under identical commands.

This paper aims to get the best of both worlds. First, using trajectory matching on real-world data optimized via a genetic algorithm (GA), it precisely estimates asymmetric joint friction and link inertia. Then, it applies domain randomization confined to a narrow, well-calibrated band around those optimized parameters. This enables the policy to develop reliable real-world adaptability without destabilizing the training process.

sections.heading: Physics identification via genetic algorithms and smooth reward design
sections.summary: Based on the robot equations of motion, direction-dependent kinetic friction, static friction, gravity compensation offsets, and inertia tensors are identified using a genetic algorithm. In the training phase, a smooth reward function penalizes Cartesian reaching errors as well as joint velocities and accelerations, allowing a TQC agent to learn torque command policies.
sections.details:
The core of this method lies in two pillars: exhaustive parameter identification (Real2Sim) and reinforcement learning design aimed at generating stable torques.

### III-A Reinforcement Learning Formulation and Reward Design
The RL agent controls a 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda, learning torque commands that guide the end-effector to a Cartesian target position within the workspace. While the goal is maximizing discounted cumulative return, the biggest hurdle in torque control is severe vibration caused by abrupt torque changes. To prevent this, the authors designed a refined reward function $r$:

In addition to a penalty term on the normalized distance $d$ to the target (weight $k_1=2$), $r$ includes suppression terms for joint angular velocities $\dot{\theta}_i$ and joint angular accelerations $\ddot{\theta}_i$. Specifically, a $\tanh$ function is applied to the velocity and acceleration penalties, and constants ($k_4=1.15, k_5=0.03, k_6=0.15$) are placed in the denominator of the acceleration term to curb runaway spikes and maintain numerical stability. As a result, the agent naturally learns to decelerate smoothly and settle precisely into place with minimal energy, rather than aggressively rushing toward the target.

### III-B Optimization Problem for Parameter Identification
Starting from the standard robot equations of motion $\tau = M(q)\ddot{q} + C(q, \dot{q})\dot{q} + G(q)$, the authors moved away from default simulator models to construct detailed, individual formulations for friction and inertia:
- Dynamic friction torque $\tau_{f,j}$: For each joint $j$, a velocity-dependent model with three coefficients $\varphi_{1,j}, \varphi_{2,j}, \varphi_{3,j}$ was adopted, accounting for directional asymmetry (positive vs. negative rotation).
- Static friction torque $\tau^{\mathrm{st}}_j$: In the low-velocity regime ($|\dot{q}_j| < \dot{q}_{\min}$), a dead-zone mechanism was implemented in simulation that cancels joint motion unless applied torques exceed a specified breakaway torque threshold.
- Minimizing trajectory error: The error function $E(\mathbf{p})$ was defined as the integrated squared error between real trajectories $\mathbf{y}_{\text{real}}(t)$ and simulated trajectories $\mathbf{y}_{\text{sim}}(t, \mathbf{p})$. A genetic algorithm (GA) was then executed to search for and optimize the parameter set $\mathbf{p}$ (link inertia tensors and joint friction parameters).

sections.heading: From algorithm comparison to hardware deployment: The decisive impact of parameter tuning
sections.summary: Comparing DDPG, SAC, TD3, and TQC revealed TQC to be the most stable, leading to its selection. GA-based identification aligned the simulator's torque response with the real robot. Policies trained in MuJoCo with domain randomization were deployed to Gazebo and the physical robot, confirming smooth, oscillation-free target reaching in hardware.
sections.details:
The experiments progressed meticulously across four phases: algorithm selection, parameter identification validation, Sim2Sim verification, and real-robot Sim2Real transfer.

First, for RL algorithm selection (Fig. 2), DDPG, SAC, TD3, and TQC were tuned via grid search and compared. TQC (Truncated Quantile Critics), which controls overestimation bias, substantially outperformed the others in average reward and showed low sensitivity to hyperparameters. Consequently, TQC was used for all subsequent experiments.

### Effects of Parameter Identification (IV-A)
Prior to identification, joint positions between simulation and hardware diverged completely due to deficient gravity compensation and unmodeled joint dynamics (Fig. 3(a), (b)). By gradually applying small torques to each joint on the real robot, the authors determined breakaway static friction torques in both directions and manually tuned gravity compensation offset torques. After applying the genetic algorithm, the joint 1 and joint 2 position curves aligned almost perfectly between the simulator and the physical robot (Fig. 3(c), (d)).

### Sim2Sim and Sim2Real Verification (IV-B, IV-C)
Training was carried out in the fast MuJoCo environment. Domain randomization was introduced by varying the 21 identified friction parameters by $\pm 10\%$ and the 42 link inertia tensor components by $\pm 5\%$. These ranges were chosen based on preliminary experiments to balance convergence speed and real-world generalizability.

Before deploying to hardware, the policy was tested in the Gazebo simulator, which uses different physics calculations (Sim2Sim). Despite a slight difference in initial reaching speed, the final rewards stably reached the same high level as MuJoCo across all target points (Fig. 4).

Finally, the policy faced the ultimate test: deployment to the real Franka Emika Panda (Sim2Real). Although the physical arm experiences unmodeled disturbances such as backlash (gear play), cable drag, and control delays, the agent guided the end-effector smoothly to random targets without a single failure and held its position stably (Fig. 8). While slight jitter was observed near the target in real trajectories, the policy operated out of the box with zero fine-tuning, validating the high fidelity of the identification and the robustness of domain randomization.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook: High-fidelity physics models unlock Sim2Real
sections.summary: By integrating GA-based dynamics identification, domain randomization, and TQC, the authors demonstrated stable Sim2Real transfer for a torque-controlled arm. Future work will extend this pipeline to contact-rich manipulation tasks, online identification, and other robotic platforms.
sections.details:
This work clearly demonstrates that meticulous physics parameter identification (Real2Sim) is a decisive factor in successful Sim2Real transfer for low-level torque-controlled robots. Rather than relying on default simulator parameters, the authors individually modeled direction-dependent friction and link inertia based on real measurements and optimized them with a genetic algorithm, dramatically boosting simulation fidelity.

Furthermore, combining a smoothness-oriented reward design with TQC alongside moderate domain randomization centered on calibrated values allowed robust control that shrugs off real-world backlash and cable drag. Stepwise validation from MuJoCo to Gazebo and finally to the real arm proved that the policy was not overfitted to any single physics engine.

Looking forward, the authors plan to expand from free-space reaching tasks to contact-rich manipulation, such as assembly tasks. They also anticipate integrating online identification to adjust system parameters during execution, as well as safety-constrained RL and compliance control for human-robot collaboration.

takeaways: In torque-controlled Sim2Real, measuring and identifying direction-dependent friction, static friction, and inertia tensors instead of trusting default URDF values is the critical factor for success.

Rather than randomizing across arbitrary, wide ranges, applying domain randomization within a tight window around accurately identified baselines (e.g., friction $\pm 10\%$, inertia $\pm 5\%$) balances training stability and real-world generalization.
For continuous torque control, TQC provides far greater stability and robustness against overestimation bias than DDPG, SAC, or TD3.
Inserting a Sim2Sim validation step between disparate simulators like MuJoCo and Gazebo before hardware deployment is an effective, practical safeguard against policy overfitting.
limitations: The evaluated task is limited to end-effector reaching in free space and does not yet validate manipulation involving harsh environmental contact or collisions.
Certain parameter identification steps, such as tuning gravity compensation torque offsets and finding breakaway static friction thresholds, still rely on manual trial and error.
Because parameter identification is conducted offline beforehand, it cannot dynamically adapt during runtime to long-term wear or changes in grease friction caused by temperature shifts.
